passages.title: The Cake That Slid Off the Plate
passages.passage:
Last month my brother Nam turned ten, and I decided to bake his birthday cake myself. I had watched my mother make sponge cakes dozens of times, so I was sure it would be easy. I found a recipe online, bought the ingredients on Saturday morning, and told everyone to stay out of the kitchen until four o'clock.

The first problem appeared almost at once. The recipe asked for three eggs, but we only had two, and the shop on our street was closed for lunch. I decided that two would be enough. Then I could not find the small measuring cup, so I guessed the amount of flour. The mixture looked a little thin, but I put it in the oven anyway and set the timer for forty minutes.

While the cake was baking, I started on the cream. This went better, and I was quite proud of the pale pink colour I had made with a few drops of strawberry juice. At that moment, however, I smelled something burning. I opened the oven door and found that the cake had risen on one side only, like a small hill, and the top was dark brown.

I cut off the burnt part, covered everything with cream, and hoped nobody would notice. Unfortunately, the cream was too soft, and by the time the guests arrived, it had slid down the sides and onto the tablecloth. Nam's friends laughed for a long time.

Nam did not mind at all. He said it was the funniest cake he had ever seen, and he ate two pieces. My mother took a photo, which is now on the fridge. Next year I will follow the recipe exactly, but I have a feeling my family will remember this cake far longer than a perfect one.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why Nam's friends laughed at his birthday party
The writer's attempt to bake a birthday cake, which went badly wrong
How the writer's mother makes birthday cakes for the family
The correct way to bake a sponge cake at home
questions.explanation: Every paragraph follows the writer's own baking attempt from confident start to sliding cream. The laughing friends and the mother's cakes are single details, not the subject.

questions.q: Why did the writer use only two eggs?
options: There were only two at home and the shop was closed
The measuring cup could not be found
The writer thought three eggs would make the mixture too thin
The recipe said that two eggs were enough
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the recipe asked for three, but 'we only had two, and the shop on our street was closed for lunch'. The missing measuring cup was a separate problem about flour.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the writer before the baking began?
options: She was nervous and asked her mother for help
She had already practised the recipe once
She had baked several cakes on her own before
She expected the job to be easy because she had watched her mother
questions.explanation: She had only watched her mother 'dozens of times' and 'was sure it would be easy' — confidence came from watching, not from her own experience.

questions.q: The word "thin" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
options: narrow
slim
watery
pale
questions.explanation: A cake mixture that is 'thin' is too liquid, not thick enough. 'Narrow' and 'slim' describe shapes and people, not a batter.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, "This went better" refers to:
options: baking the cake
making the cream
setting the timer
finding the strawberry juice
questions.explanation: The sentence before says 'I started on the cream', so 'This' is the cream-making, which is contrasted with the cake that was burning.

questions.q: The guests arrived before the cream slid off the cake.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'by the time the guests arrived, it had slid down the sides' — the past perfect shows the sliding happened first.

questions.q: Nam's friends brought him presents.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says the friends laughed at the cake, but nothing at all is said about presents.

passages.title: A Dragon Over the Rice Fields
passages.passage:
Every year, at the end of the dry season, the village where my grandparents live holds a kite festival on the wide field behind the pagoda. This year my cousin Linh and I were finally old enough to enter the children's competition, so we spent two weekends building our kite.

We chose a simple diamond shape because Grandpa said beginners should not try anything fancy. He showed us how to split bamboo into thin strips and bend them over a candle flame until they curved without breaking. The frame took a whole afternoon. For the covering we used strong paper that Linh painted with a red and yellow dragon. The most difficult part was attaching the flute. Many kites in our village carry a small bamboo flute that sings when the wind passes through it, and each family has its own sound.

On the day of the festival, the field was full of people by seven in the morning. There were kites shaped like fish, birds and butterflies, and one enormous kite that needed four men to hold it. The judges did not only look at how high a kite could fly. They also gave points for how steady it was, how beautiful it looked and, for flute kites, how clear the sound was.

Our first launch failed. The wind dropped just as Linh let go, and the kite fell into the grass. Grandpa told us to wait and watch the flags on the pagoda. When they began to move again, we ran, and this time the dragon climbed quickly and stayed up for the whole ten minutes.

We did not win. The first prize went to a girl from the next village whose kite carried three flutes that played together like a tiny band. But walking home with Grandpa, holding our slightly torn dragon, I felt as if we had.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Two cousins building a kite and entering it in a village festival
How judges decide the winner of a kite competition
Why a girl from the next village won the first prize
The history of flute kites in Vietnamese villages
questions.explanation: The passage follows Linh and the writer from building the kite to flying it at the festival. The judging rules and the winner are details from single paragraphs.

questions.q: What did Grandpa show the children how to do?
options: Attach a bamboo flute to the frame
Bend strips of bamboo over a flame
Hold a very large kite in a strong wind
Paint a dragon on strong paper
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: he 'showed us how to split bamboo into thin strips and bend them over a candle flame'. Linh did the painting, and the flute was simply 'the most difficult part'.

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, what did the judges consider?
options: How quickly a kite could be launched
Only how high each kite could fly
Height, steadiness, beauty and, for some kites, sound
How many people were needed to hold the kite
questions.explanation: The judges 'did not only look at how high a kite could fly' but gave points for steadiness, beauty and, for flute kites, the sound. Option A is exactly what the passage denies.

questions.q: The word "steady" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
options: quiet
fast
bright
stable
questions.explanation: A 'steady' kite stays in one position without shaking or dropping — it is stable in the air.

questions.q: In paragraph 4, "they" in "When they began to move again" refers to:
options: the flags on the pagoda
Linh and the writer
the other kites
the judges
questions.explanation: Grandpa told them to 'watch the flags on the pagoda'; the flags moving again showed that the wind had returned.

questions.q: Why does the writer say "I felt as if we had" at the end?
options: The judges later changed their decision
The writer was proud of what they had achieved, even without a prize
Grandpa had promised to buy them a prize
The writer believed the girl's kite had cheated
questions.explanation: 'We did not win' is followed by 'I felt as if we had' — the feeling of winning came from the successful flight and the walk home with Grandpa, not from any prize.

questions.q: Linh and the writer had taken part in the competition in earlier years.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says they were 'finally old enough to enter' this year, so this was their first time.

passages.title: Twenty Minutes on Foot
passages.passage:
When our family moved to a smaller town last year, my parents made a decision I did not like at all. Instead of driving me to school, as they had done in the city, they told me I would walk. The school was only two kilometres away, and Dad said that was a perfectly reasonable distance for a fourteen-year-old.

For the first week I complained every morning. It was hot, my bag was heavy, and I arrived with my shirt sticking to my back. My mother's answer was to give me a lighter bag and a bottle of water, and to wake me ten minutes earlier so that I did not have to rush.

Slowly, the walk stopped feeling like a punishment. I found a route through a small park where an old man practised tai chi every morning; after a month, he began to nod to me as I passed. I noticed that the bakery on Tran Phu Street opened at half past six and that the bread smelled best at twenty to seven. I also discovered that two girls from my class lived on the same road, and we started walking together. Now we test each other on vocabulary on the way to school and talk about everything else on the way home.

There were practical changes too. I sleep better, and my PE teacher says I run faster than I did in September. The money my parents have saved on petrol goes into a jar, and at the end of the year we are going to spend it on a trip to the beach.

I still take the bus when it rains heavily, and I would not pretend that every morning is pleasant. But when my aunt visited last month and offered to drive me, I surprised everyone, including myself, by saying no.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why the writer's family moved from the city to a smaller town
The dangers of walking to school in hot weather
How the writer's family saved money for a beach holiday
How the writer's feelings about walking to school changed over time
questions.explanation: The passage moves from 'I complained every morning' to saying no to a lift — the change of attitude is the thread. The move and the holiday money are background details.

questions.q: How did the writer's mother respond to the complaints?
options: She bought the writer a bus ticket for the whole year
She agreed to drive the writer on hot days
She gave the writer a lighter bag, water and an earlier wake-up time
She found two classmates to walk with the writer
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists exactly these three things. The classmates were discovered by the writer, and the bus is only used in heavy rain.

questions.q: The word "rush" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
options: wait
hurry
wake
worry
questions.explanation: Being woken ten minutes earlier means there is enough time, so the writer does not need to 'rush' — to move in a hurry.

questions.q: In paragraph 1, "that" in "Dad said that was a perfectly reasonable distance" refers to:
options: two kilometres
driving to school
being fourteen years old
the smaller town
questions.explanation: The previous clause says the school 'was only two kilometres away', and 'that' picks up this distance.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention the PE teacher in paragraph 4?
options: To explain why the writer sleeps better
To complain that PE lessons have become harder
To show that the writer now wants to become an athlete
To give evidence of a physical benefit of walking
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about 'practical changes'; the teacher's comment that the writer runs faster is proof of one such change.

questions.q: The writer walks to school in every kind of weather.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5: 'I still take the bus when it rains heavily', so not every day is a walking day.

questions.q: The writer's aunt lives in the same town as the family.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: We only know the aunt 'visited last month' and offered a lift; where she lives is never mentioned.

passages.title: A Rabbit Called Banh Bao
passages.passage:
My sister An had wanted a pet for years, but our flat is small and our parents always said no to a dog. Then, last spring, a neighbour who was moving abroad asked if we could take her rabbit. Mum agreed on one condition: An had to look after it herself, and if she stopped, the rabbit would go to another family.

The rabbit was white with grey ears, round and soft, so An named him Banh Bao after the steamed bun he looked like. We had imagined that a rabbit would simply sit quietly in a cage, but Banh Bao had other ideas. Within a week he had learned to push the cage door open with his nose. We would come home to find him under the sofa or, once, sitting proudly in the middle of the dining table.

An read everything she could find about rabbits. She learned that they should not live on carrots alone, as cartoons suggest, but need mainly hay and fresh green leaves. She learned that rabbits hate being lifted, so she taught herself to sit on the floor and let him come to her. She also found out that they chew almost anything, which explained the marks on the leg of Dad's chair and the hole in my phone charger.

The biggest change, though, was in An herself. She used to leave her homework until the last minute, but a pet that needs feeding at the same time every day forced her to make a timetable, and the habit spread to her schoolwork. Her teacher noticed the difference before our parents did.

Banh Bao is now a full member of the family. He sleeps at the end of An's bed, and he thumps his back foot loudly whenever the doorbell rings. Mum, who was the least keen at the start, is the one who talks to him most.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The damage a rabbit can do to furniture in a small flat
The correct diet for a pet rabbit
How a family took in a rabbit and what changed as a result
Why the writer's parents refused to buy a dog
questions.explanation: The passage covers how Banh Bao arrived, how An learned to care for him, and how An and the family changed. Diet, the dog and the chewed furniture are each only part of one paragraph.

questions.q: What condition did Mum set before accepting the rabbit?
options: An had to read a book about rabbits first
An had to keep the rabbit in its cage at all times
The neighbour had to take the rabbit back after one year
An had to care for the rabbit herself or it would be given away
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'An had to look after it herself, and if she stopped, the rabbit would go to another family'. The reading was An's own idea later.

questions.q: What does paragraph 2 suggest about Banh Bao?
options: He was cleverer and more active than the family expected
He preferred to stay quietly in his cage
He was unwell when he arrived
He was frightened of the family at first
questions.explanation: The family 'had imagined' a quiet rabbit in a cage, but within a week he could open the door with his nose and was found on the dining table — he surprised them.

questions.q: The word "keen" in the last paragraph is closest in meaning to:
options: careful
enthusiastic
worried
quiet
questions.explanation: Mum was 'the least keen at the start' but now talks to him most — the contrast shows 'keen' means enthusiastic or eager.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention the phone charger in paragraph 3?
options: To show that the writer dislikes the rabbit
To complain that An does not control her pet
To give an example of the rabbit chewing things
To explain why the family needed a new cage
questions.explanation: It follows 'they chew almost anything, which explained…' — the chair leg and the charger are two examples of that chewing.

questions.q: The rabbit was given to the family by a relative.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the rabbit came from 'a neighbour who was moving abroad', not a relative.

questions.q: An now gets higher marks at school.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says An's timetable habit spread to her schoolwork and her teacher noticed a difference, but nothing is said about her marks.
